content:
when a photo or any file is deleted, the pointer will no longer be pointing to that perticular location in the memory but the content will still be present, but the data in that location can still be overridden (meaning replacing with new data). once the data is overridden you cant recover the old data that was present there. this is how storage works.
There is no concept of deletion of data, just data wont be pointed or data will be overridden.

content: What the hell is he/she talking about, ever single thing we store in our system it take space in our rom as we all know, and let suppose you deleted some file then what would happen ? Guess ? Well the area where you stored your file will become free means kernal will tell os that "bro now start showing extra space in the UI" so that user would think ok now i got back my 1 GB space after deleting file, but the thing is your file is still there, but now your os know that if you download any file then that file re-write a area where your first file was stored, so it means if you delete something and after that if you don't do anything that re-writes the data you can still retrieve it, and it is possible using some software (you can google search for this). But if you do any activity that re-writes that area(like downloading something) then it is impossible to retrive deleted data. So in short "delete karne jaesi cheej hoti hai" don't listen to these morons.

content:
Stop please:

If you're not using cloud storage, your images and other data are stored locally on your device. When you delete an image, it usually goes to a "Recently Deleted" or "Trash" folder, where it stays for a while before being permanently deleted. Even after permanent deletion, the data isn't immediately removed from your phone's storage. Instead, the space is marked as available for new data to overwrite it. Until something overwrites that space, the deleted image can often be recovered using specialized data recovery tools.

However, if you're not using cloud storage and you permanently delete an image, it eventually gets overwritten and becomes much harder (though not always impossible) to recover. The concept of a digital footprint still applies because traces of deleted data can linger in various forms, and recovery might be possible depending on how the device manages storage.

So usually operating systems only disassociate the memory address of the data so that the area is now available to be written on for new data. Hence the recovery apps will only be able to recover if that portion of the memory is not overwritten by any new data.

Wrong information. When you delete something, data will remain till you add new data in it's place.

Example: if you delete a 4 mb pic from a 64 gb memory card, which is full with other data, once you add another 4 mb new pic or any other data, you actually deleted old one permanently. Nobody can retrieve it. 

So, if you are very conscious about your data being retrieved in future, just fill your memory with any movie files and delete those movie files. To be sure, do it two to three times. I assure you, not even high grade data recovery company can retrieve your old data.

title: How to fix your Google storage space forever... for free!
content: So I'm an amateur videographer. Each time I do an event, I would upload the footage to my Google Drive and then share it with the client. However this wasn't working out so good because the files would be eating up my storage. And after leaving the footage on my Drive for over a month I delete it and very next day the client wants to know where it went. So, I came up with a new system. Each time I do an event, I make a new Google account (sometimes two) based on the name of the event or the client, and upload the footage to that Drive. I then share the username and password with the client giving them full control of the account to do what they want with. Now the footage is not taking up my space nor the client's space and can stay there for eternity (or until Google decides to remove unused accounts etc...) I think it's a pretty smart idea.

content: Good plan Neil, but with one small catch! When you set up a new account and tell it to backup your photos, it will backup ALL the photos that are stored on your phone, not just the most recent year, which could mean several year's worth, so you'll be in the same position you were when you started. If you want an account for each year, for example, you'd need to make sure your phone ONLY had this year's photos on it. Then you'd need to delete them all from your phone before starting a new account for the next year. Also beware some services sync rather than backup, which means when you delete on your phone, it deletes them online too. The moral being to always backup photos onto a separate physical drive somewhere before doing anything clever!

You can use google photos with backup on (express settings) that will backup the photos and videos in SD(lower) quality but will save your google cloud storage.

I also suffered from the same issue of yours and used teh express settings.
Alternatively, you can create another google account and backup some media folders to that account and others to your main account which would practically give you a plenty of 30GB(15+15) of storage for media files.
I hope this helps....

title: I Moved to Immich… Can It Really Replace Google Photos?
content:
Definitely curious about this.  Two immediate questions come to mind: 

1) Lock-in.  Is there a reasonably simple way to export my images, once added, in a platform neutral manner, so I could bring them into a different system at some point in the future when immich no longer meets my needs?

2) Keywording.  Machine learning searches can be fantastic, but even with simple criteria, we all know they aren't perfect.  And then there is the custom criteria: If I want to search something hyper-specific to my hobbies and life, mass-market AI is not going to know that this particular doohickey is this very specific thing, and I'm going to want search for it later.  If I can manually add keywords, that makes a HUGE difference.

I'll do my own research, but I thought I'd throw this out for others to consider.  Especially with that last bit, Apple and other companies love to show that I can search my photos for "cake" or "palm trees" to see photos with palm trees, or photos of cakes.  But when I want to see the photos of code cylinders and belt boxes, being able to search those terms for my specific tags would yield very different results (including that fuzzy shot of the inside of the box I took, which shows an important detail but is not really recognizable as a "box" in that pic) than just letting the machine show me what it things people want to see.

title: I Moved to Immich… Can It Really Replace Google Photos?
content: I tried to migrate from iCloud to Immich, but clearly it’s designed more as a backup than a true alternative. From mobile you can’t upload photos directly to an album, you can only dump them into a timeline or sync folders. I don’t want to sync folders and now manage them in two places. You can upload directly to an album from the web UI, but there’s no “select all”, so it’s not easy to upload thousands of photos. It also seems to abstract file structure away from you, with a Postgres database containing all the organizational data, which makes it not very portable. I decided to use my UGREEN NAS’ built in Photo app which seems superior in every way. And it supports pet recognition which is big for me

title: 🤩 Google Pixel 8 Photography: iPhones Can’t Do This!
content:
As a guy who has an iPhone 13 and a Pixel 7, I would pick the Pixel for photos and the iPhone for videos.

However, if I had to pick just one of the two (only for the camera), I would pick the iPhone as it is more consistent. With the Pixel you get really great shots, but you also get some very mediocre night time (and tough lighting condition) shots. With the iPhone, you get fewer pictures that blow your mind but fewer still that disappoint you.

Having said that, I prefer the Pixel overall in my day to day usage (as a phone/media consumption device). The only other area where the iPhone outperforms the Pixel is app optimisation (especially social media), and security.

TLDR: Both are great. Don't be a fanboy. Pick your phone based on your preferred OS and your usage.
